LESSON 48 OF 106·Identity, Authentication and Access Control

Authorisation vs Authentication: Least Privilege in Practice

Why 'who are you' and 'what may you do' have to be answered separately — deny by default, least privilege, and the failures that leave signed-in users over-privileged.

Foundation13 min
Why this matters

Authentication and authorisation are different questions, and most serious application breaches are authorisation failures rather than authentication ones. Broken access control has ranked first in the most recent industry survey for exactly this reason.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Authentication asks who this is. Authorisation asks whether this identity may perform this action on this resource.
  • The correct authorisation decision needs the identity, the action and the specific object, not just the route.
  • Default-deny means a request is rejected unless a rule explicitly allows it, which is the safer default.
  • Least privilege means each identity receives only the access its task requires, and no more.
  • Enforcement belongs on the server for every request, because the client is under the user control.

The background

  • Early applications checked authentication in the interface and assumed that was sufficient.
  • As APIs grew, authorisation moved to the server, but was often implemented per endpoint, which led to inconsistent rules.
  • The industry survey began ranking broken access control as a leading category, which changed what teams prioritised.
  • Centralised policy engines emerged so authorisation decisions could be written once and applied consistently.

Real-world examples

  • Hiding a delete button in the interface leaves the endpoint available, and the request can be sent directly.
  • A record identifier in a request is often treated as proof of permission, which lets one user reach another data.
  • An endpoint that checks only that a user is logged in, and not which records belong to them, is a very common flaw.

What to look for

  • Check whether every endpoint that touches a specific object verifies permission for that object.
  • Check for authorisation enforced only in the client, which is not enforcement.
  • Check whether a role can be supplied by the user, since a client-supplied role is not a decision.
  • Check that denied requests are logged, because silent denial is how these flaws persist.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Default to deny and grant explicitly, so a forgotten rule fails safely.
  • Check permission on the object being acted on, not only on the route being called.
  • Keep authorisation decisions on the server and repeat them on every request.
  • Centralise policy so endpoints cannot quietly implement contradictory rules.
  • Test with two accounts of different privilege, which finds these flaws faster than any scanner.
